identification.summary: HURRICANE PANDA is CrowdStrike's name for a China-based adversary whose intrusions CrowdStrike says it has investigated since 2013, including at several large telecommunications and technology companies [S2]. Its preferred initial access and persistence is a China Chopper webshell, followed by credential theft with a tool such as Mimikatz [S2]. In October 2014 CrowdStrike reported the group using a 64-bit Windows privilege-escalation zero-day, CVE-2014-4113 [S1].
identification.notes: CrowdStrike name only. No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name is recorded in this encyclopedia for this actor. Search results for other aggregators (Malpedia, MISP Galaxy) listed it alongside other Chinese-nexus groups, but no cited source here states an alias, so none is added.

attribution.confidence: CrowdStrike describes the group as China-based [S2]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Vendor investigation by CrowdStrike across multiple customer intrusions [S2]. The basis for the China assessment was not visible in the material reviewed.

targeting.notes: CrowdStrike says it fought the group at several large telecommunications and technology companies and in April 2015 described defending two customers [S2][S3]. Regions and customer names were not found.

capabilities.summary: Initial access via a China Chopper webshell, a roughly 70-byte eval() text file uploaded through SQL injection or WebDAV vulnerabilities on web servers [S2]. Post-compromise the group runs a repacked credential theft tool such as Mimikatz and, with administrator credentials, moves laterally using 'net use' and 'wmic' commands through the webshell [S2]. CrowdStrike reported use of a 64-bit Windows local privilege-escalation zero-day, CVE-2014-4113, in October 2014 [S1]. CrowdStrike described itself as having reported this to Microsoft for patching [S3]. Secondary reporting of CrowdStrike's findings also mentions PlugX and free DNS services, but those details were not confirmed in a primary page I could open.

campaigns.name: Intrusions at telecommunications and technology companies
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike began investigating HURRICANE PANDA intrusions in 2013 and describes ongoing battles at several large telecom and technology firms.

campaigns.name: CVE-2014-4113 zero-day use
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike reported the group's use of a 64-bit Windows privilege-escalation zero-day.

campaigns.name: Long-running campaign reportedly halted
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike's chief of technology said on a public mailing list that the group stopped a multi-year campaign against two Falcon customers; a participant questioned whether this reflected a detection blind spot.

diamond.adversary: China-based group tracked by CrowdStrike; sponsor not established in sources [S2].
diamond.capability: China Chopper webshell, Mimikatz, net use/wmic lateral movement, CVE-2014-4113 zero-day [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Internet-facing web servers compromised via SQL injection or WebDAV flaws serve as footholds [S2]. Actor-controlled C2 details not found.
diamond.technology: Exposed web applications with injection or WebDAV weaknesses, and unpatched Windows privilege-escalation flaws [S1][S2].

gaps: Could not open the CrowdStrike blog posts directly (fetch failed); S1 and S2 content comes from the existing encyclopedia record text and search-result summaries. Re-verify against the primary posts.
No sponsor, state organization, or government attribution found.
Aliases and overlap with other vendor clusters are unconfirmed; do not merge with Deep Panda, APT19, or others without a cited source.
No activity found after 2015; whether the cluster is still tracked or was merged into a newer CrowdStrike name is unknown.
Dark Reading, SCMP, Malpedia and FireEye coverage of the zero-day surfaced in searches but were not opened or dated, so are not cited.
Specific victims, regions, objectives and infrastructure are not public in the material gathered.
